newsitem.title: USA: U.S. labor mkt pressure eases, favorable for rates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. labor mkt pressure eases, favorable for rates.

text.p: A rising unemployment rate in June packed with another dose of benign inflation data marked evidence of a significant economic slowdown from a heady first quarter pace, economists said.
The data, which also posted a lower-than-expected rise in nonfarm payrolls of 217,000, was called favorable for near-term interest rate policy.
"The best news...is you have a little less pressure in the labor markets with the unemployment rate increasing from 4.8 to 5.0 percent," said Hugh Johnson of First Albany Corp.
Also in the report, average hourly earnings rose by $0.04, or 0.3 percent, to $12.22. The average workweek lengthened slightly to 34.7 from 34.6, the government said.

Analysts polled by Reuters forecasted a 222,000 rise in payrolls for June. Payrolls grew a revised 166,000 in May, the Labor Department reported. The unemployment rate was forecast at a steady 4.8 percent.

Johnson, who is chief investment officer at First Albany Corp, remarked that worker earnings assuaged market fears that inflation would follow the long-standing tightness of the labor market. It also affirmed the second quarter slowdown suggested in other key indicators of the past two months.

"This report is consistent with the National Association of Purchasing Managers survey, which said the slowdown that began in April has continued into June and there's not much evidence of the kind of upward pressure on wages that would lead to higher consumer inflation," Johnson said.
Indeed, Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, said the data presents a healthy, non-inflationary economic picture. She cited a benefits of a looser job market.
"With the unemployment rate going up, it seems clear that economic growth has moderated to a more sustainable level," Katz said.

James Padinha, economist at Briefing.com, said the non-threatening earnings increase and higher jobless rate combined with the longer workweek and still-strong job creation outlines a divergence in the data. The market is taking the soft inflation data to heart, he said, but it should not be forgotten the economy is growing strongly.

June's non-farm payroll gain of 217,000, while below many economists' estimates, marks no deceleration from the 12-month moving average of 212,000, Padinha said. And the longer workweek will inevitably translate into some wage gains, he added.

Analysts noted the common outlook for two percent or lower Q2 gross domestic product is in sharp contrast to the 5.9 percent Q1 rate, but that growth still averages out above the level said to be acceptable to the Federal Reserve.

Growth for the first half should average near a strong four percent, Padinha said. Another economist questioned how long the Fed would be able to ignore "very solid job growth which is helping boost consumer confidence to all time highs."
At least some of the first quarter's strength was "borrowed" from the second quarter, analysts noted.
"In order to get (growth) below four percent, and this is the bull's argument, you'd have to get trend growth for the second half," Padinha said, adding that he does not believe that will happen.
"Income growth is still great, confidence - everyone says they feel great, and the risk is that we'd get a bigger than trend growth in the second half," he said.
But analysts conceded the Federal Reserve has stood tight in the midst of strong growth for a long time now -- thanks to the absence of inflation.
